intro: The Hanuman Chalisa is a devotional composition of forty verses (chalisa means 'forty') in praise of Hanuman, the devoted companion of Lord Rama. It is attributed to the poet-saint Tulsidas, who lived in the sixteenth century and is also known for his retelling of the Ramayana in Awadhi, the Ramcharitmanas. The text opens with a short invocation to the poet's guru before turning entirely to Hanuman's qualities, deeds and devotion. It is written in simple, rhythmic Awadhi verse meant to be recited aloud rather than studied silently. Over the centuries it has become one of the most widely recited hymns in North Indian households, recited by people of varied backgrounds regardless of formal ritual training. What follows is an explanation of what each portion of the verses conveys and how the recitation is traditionally practised, not a line-by-line rendering of the text itself.

groups.heading: The opening invocation
groups.body: Before addressing Hanuman, Tulsidas first bows to the dust of his guru's feet, saying that cleaning the mirror of his own mind with it allows him to describe the pure glory of Rama, which he says yields the four fruits (the four traditional aims of life). He then calls himself weak in understanding and turns to Hanuman, son of the wind, asking for strength, wisdom and knowledge, and for relief from faults and afflictions. These two preliminary couplets set the tone for the whole hymn: it is framed as a humble request rather than a boast of ability, and it establishes Hanuman as the one being addressed throughout.

groups.heading: Praise of Hanuman's nature
groups.body: The verses that follow salute Hanuman as an ocean of wisdom and virtue, famous across the three worlds, and as the messenger of Rama possessing unmatched strength. He is named as the son of Anjani and of the wind god Pavan. Here the Hanuman Chalisa is simply laying out who Hanuman is in relation to Rama and to his own parentage, establishing the figure the rest of the hymn will describe in more physical and narrative detail.

groups.heading: Description of his form
groups.body: This section paints a picture of Hanuman's appearance — his great strength and heroic bearing, his golden-coloured body, earrings and curled hair, the mace and banner in his hands, and the sacred thread across his shoulder. It also calls him the son of Shankar and the delight of Kesari, noting his brilliance and the reverence he commands across the world. This passage is descriptive rather than narrative; it gives the devotee a mental image to hold while reciting the Hanuman Chalisa.

groups.heading: His learning and eagerness to serve
groups.body: The text then speaks of Hanuman's learning, virtue and sharpness of mind, and of his eagerness to carry out Rama's work. It says he delights in hearing of his lord's deeds and that Rama, Lakshman and Sita dwell in his heart. This group of verses shifts the emphasis from physical description to character, presenting devotion and readiness to serve as central to who Hanuman is in this hymn.

groups.heading: Episodes from the Rama story
groups.body: Several verses recall specific moments associated with Hanuman within the Ramayana narrative: taking a subtle form to show himself to Sita, taking a fearsome form to burn Lanka, and taking a mighty form to destroy demons in service of Rama's cause. Another verse recalls him bringing the sanjivani herb that revives Lakshman, after which Rama embraces him with joy. The Hanuman Chalisa does not narrate these episodes in full; it refers to them briefly, assuming the listener already knows the larger story of the Ramayana.

groups.heading: Rama's regard for Hanuman
groups.body: Following the sanjivani episode, the verses describe Rama praising Hanuman highly, saying he is as dear as his own brother Bharat. It is said that even the thousand-headed serpent Sheshnag sings his praises, and Rama draws him close in affection. This short section underlines the depth of the bond between Rama and Hanuman that runs through the whole hymn, presenting Hanuman's devotion as answered by Rama's own regard.

groups.heading: Recognition by sages and gods
groups.body: The next verses mention that sages such as the four Kumaras, Brahma and other divine figures, along with Narada, Saraswati and Sheshnag, along with Yama, Kubera and the guardians of the directions, find it difficult to fully describe Hanuman's glory, and that poets and scholars too fall short. This passage situates Hanuman's stature as recognised beyond the human world, among sages and celestial figures, within the devotional logic of the Hanuman Chalisa.

groups.heading: Help given to Sugriva
groups.body: A further verse recalls that Hanuman helped Sugriva, bringing about his meeting with Rama and his restoration to the throne of Kishkindha. Like the earlier episodes, this is mentioned briefly as one of the services Hanuman is remembered for, continuing the pattern of the Hanuman Chalisa recalling his deeds one after another as reasons for the praise being offered to him.

recitation: The Hanuman Chalisa is commonly recited on Tuesdays and Saturdays, days traditionally associated with Hanuman in North Indian practice, and especially during the festival of Hanuman Jayanti, which marks his birth. Many people recite it as part of a daily routine, often in the morning after bathing, or in the evening at a household shrine, standing or sitting before an image or picture of Hanuman. It is usually recited aloud, sometimes with a lit lamp and incense, and sometimes along with a simple offering such as flowers or sweets. Some people recite it once, others undertake a count of multiple repetitions, such as eleven or one hundred and eight times, particularly during a vow or a period of focused practice. It is often recited together with the Hanuman Ashtak or the Bajrang Baan in some households, though it also stands on its own as a complete hymn. Because its Awadhi is simple and rhythmic, it is frequently among the first devotional texts people learn by heart, including children, and group recitation in temples or community gatherings on Tuesdays is common in many parts of India.
tradition: Within the devotional tradition that has grown around the Hanuman Chalisa, it is held to be a hymn of praise and remembrance rather than a set of instructions or predictions. Tulsidas presents it as an appeal to Hanuman for strength, wisdom and relief from distress, and this framing is why the hymn is widely recited in moments when people seek steadiness or courage. Tradition associates Hanuman with protection, discipline and unwavering devotion to Rama, and the Hanuman Chalisa is recited as an expression of seeking these same qualities through remembrance of him. Some households recite it as part of daily worship regardless of circumstance, treating it simply as a regular devotional habit rather than a response to any particular need. The text itself does not claim specific outcomes; what is said about its effects comes from long-standing practice and oral tradition passed down through generations of reciters, rather than from the verses making explicit promises.

faq.a: It is attributed to Tulsidas, a poet-saint who lived in the sixteenth century and is also known for composing the Ramcharitmanas, a retelling of the Ramayana in Awadhi. The Hanuman Chalisa is written in the same language and devotional style, addressed directly to Hanuman.

Chalisa comes from the word for forty, referring to the forty main verses of praise that make up the hymn, framed by two introductory couplets at the start. This structure is common to other chalisa compositions dedicated to different deities as well.

faq.q: Is there a fixed number of times I should recite it?
faq.a: There is no single fixed rule. Many people recite the Hanuman Chalisa once during daily worship, while others follow traditional counts such as eleven or one hundred and eight repetitions, especially during a vow or on Tuesdays and Saturdays. The choice generally follows personal or family custom.

faq.q: Can the Hanuman Chalisa be recited by anyone, or are there restrictions?
faq.a: In most households it is recited freely by anyone, including children, without requiring special initiation or ritual training. Customs around cleanliness or timing vary by family and region, so it is reasonable to follow whatever practice one has grown up with or feels comfortable adopting.

faq.q: Does the text explain the story of Hanuman and Rama in full?
faq.a: No, the Hanuman Chalisa only refers briefly to episodes such as the burning of Lanka or the bringing of the sanjivani herb, assuming familiarity with the fuller narrative found in texts like the Ramayana. It functions as praise built on references rather than as a complete narrative account.
